# Audit the Queue, Not Just the Score

Algorithmic audits usually begin with a model: its training data, error rates, feature weights, and outputs. That approach makes sense when a score directly determines an outcome. Yet many operational systems do not make final decisions. They rank cases for later attention by inspectors, technicians, or clerks. In these settings, the order of a queue may matter more than whether any individual score is accurate. Auditors should therefore treat queue behavior—not merely model performance—as a primary object of examination.

Consider PatchRank, an illustrative system used by the fictional city of Marrowick to prioritize reports of damaged sidewalks. The model estimates the probability that each defect will cause an injury within thirty days. A report with a score of 0.61 enters the queue above one scoring 0.58. On paper, PatchRank can be well calibrated: among every hundred reports scored near 0.60, roughly sixty may involve a hazardous defect. It can also show similar accuracy across districts. Neither result establishes that residents receive comparable service. If work crews repeatedly clear the top fifth of the queue while lower-ranked reports remain pending, small differences in scores can become large differences in waiting time.

The problem grows when the queue changes after scoring. Marrowick might allow council offices to flag urgent cases, supervisors to combine duplicate reports, and crews to select nearby jobs to reduce travel. Rain may generate new cases faster than staff can close old ones. A report’s eventual position would then reflect a sequence of human and technical interventions, not PatchRank alone. An audit confined to model outputs could certify the scoring system while overlooking the process that residents actually encounter.

A queue audit should reconstruct that process. For each case, auditors would record its initial score, every change in rank, the rule or person responsible for the change, its waiting time, and its final disposition. They should examine rank volatility as well as average delay. If reports from one district frequently fall after each nightly update, that pattern deserves attention even when the model’s district-level error rates look equal. Auditors should also compare cases near operational cutoffs. Two almost identical hazards placed on opposite sides of the daily crew limit provide more useful evidence about service consequences than a broad comparison of all high- and low-scoring reports.

This approach offers a practical benefit: it assigns responsibility more precisely. Suppose PatchRank gives comparable scores to similar defects, but reports submitted by telephone take two extra days to enter the system. The remedy is not necessarily to retrain the model. It may be to alter data-entry staffing. If supervisors routinely promote cases accompanied by detailed photographs, the city might need clearer escalation rules rather than a new fairness constraint. By separating scoring, ingestion, reranking, and execution, a queue audit can prevent every operational failure from being mislabeled an algorithmic failure.

Cities and firms could implement this through a simple Queue Audit Standard. Any system that ranks more cases than staff can promptly process would retain six months of rank histories and publish three measures: median waiting time by intake channel, the share of cases moved by manual intervention, and the proportion of near-cutoff cases completed within the stated service period. A quarterly sample of fifty cases would then be traced from submission to completion. Systems exceeding a 20 percent waiting-time gap between channels would require a corrective plan. These requirements are modest enough for routine procurement contracts and concrete enough to discourage audits made up only of general assurances.

There are objections. Logging every change creates storage costs, and named records of staff interventions could encourage defensive behavior. Expanding an audit beyond the model can also blur accountability: a vendor may blame the agency’s workflow, while the agency blames the ranking tool. These concerns support careful access controls and common event labels, not a return to model-only review. An immutable log can identify whether a change came from a software rule, a supervisor, or a capacity constraint without making every employee’s identity public. Audit contracts can then allocate responsibility by stage.

A stronger objection is that queue measures can distract from severe model defects. An inaccurate hazard model should not escape scrutiny merely because waiting times are evenly distributed. Queue auditing must therefore supplement conventional tests of accuracy, robustness, and disparate error, rather than replace them. Even so, conventional testing should lose its privileged status. In a constrained service, the central question is not simply, “Did the model estimate risk correctly?” It is, “What happened to a case because this system placed it here, at this time, among these competing cases?”

The distinction matters because ranking systems exercise power through delay. A case does not need to be formally rejected to be neglected; it can remain perpetually below tomorrow’s work limit. Auditors who examine only scores may validate an elegant component while missing that outcome. Following cases through the queue would make audits less tidy, but it would bring them closer to the decisions that ranking systems actually shape.
planted_strengths: Advances a distinctive and relevant thesis that ranking and delay should be audited as operational outcomes, not treated as incidental to model evaluation.
Uses a concrete fictional sidewalk-repair system to explain how calibrated scores can still produce unequal waiting times.
Distinguishes several stages—intake, scoring, reranking, and execution—which supports more precise assignment of responsibility.
Offers actionable audit elements, including rank histories, near-cutoff comparisons, intervention logs, and waiting-time measures.
Acknowledges meaningful objections concerning cost, staff surveillance, blurred accountability, and the danger of neglecting conventional model testing.
planted_weaknesses: The central claim that queue behavior may matter more than model performance is asserted from an illustrative example rather than supported with empirical evidence or a broader range of cases.
The proposed six-month retention period, sample of fifty cases, and 20 percent gap threshold are arbitrary and not justified statistically or operationally.
The essay treats intake-channel waiting-time gaps as suspicious without adequately accounting for legitimate differences in case complexity, verification needs, or reporting quality.
Its proposed metrics are too narrow to capture recurring backlog, seasonal demand, strategic reranking, or harms hidden within aggregate medians.
The response to implementation objections is incomplete: immutable logs and event labels do not by themselves resolve privacy, gaming, vendor access, or causal attribution problems.
quality_rationale: The essay is coherent, original, and practically oriented, with a non-obvious focus on queue dynamics as an audit object. Its fictional example clearly demonstrates the mechanism, and the lifecycle framing plus counterargument section gives the position useful depth. However, the proposal relies on unsupported thresholds and a single illustrative setting, while several metrics and implementation claims are underdeveloped. Those limitations weaken the general argument enough to keep the work near the middle of the scale despite its strong organizing idea.
title: Audit the Queue, Not Just the Score
topic: Why audits of algorithmic ranking systems should trace queue movement and waiting time alongside model accuracy.
